10 Session Replay Tools for Mobile for Product Teams & Devs
Session Replay
BY Begüm Aykut
Almost all session replay tools for mobile apps include the following features:
Video-like playback of taps, gestures, and screen transitions
Rage tap / dead tap detection
Crash/error context tied to the replay
Auto-marked event timeline (errors, rage clicks) with jump-to navigation
Skip-inactivity / auto-fast-forward through idle time
From there, most session replay tools fall into one of two categories depending on what other features are bundled along with them:
Platforms for product teams that also offer features for analyzing user behavior like funnels, heatmaps, and event analytics, so teams can go from "this metric dropped" to "here's why," using replay to explain patterns across segments of users rather than a single incident.
Platforms for engineering teams that also include features for understanding and fixing what was happening on the backend rather than just what the user was doing on the screen, including feature flags, error tracking, console logs, network requests, traces, and API calls.
In this guide, we’ll cover options for both categories, starting with an in-depth look at UXCam, our mobile-first session replay tool built for product teams.
Ready to stop guessing why users drop off? Schedule a demo or try UXCam for free , get started in 5 minutes, and start learning the why behind user behavior.
UXCam: Mobile-first session replay built for non-technical teams
We built UXCam as a mobile-first product and UX analytics platform with built-in session replay tools , heatmaps , funnels , customer journey maps , technical issue analytics , and an integrated AI analyst .
There are a few ways that our session replay tool for mobile is different from other solutions:
Unlike other tools that started by supporting web apps, we started with mobile apps first, which means you get accurate, fast playback in an ultralight SDK that supports most mobile frameworks.
Anyone, even non-developers, can create and track events within minutes, and find past sessions using those events rather than waiting for developers to do it for you and for new sessions to roll in.
UXCam offers privacy controls, regional hosting options, and contractual safeguards that can support GDPR compliance and company privacy requirements.
You can choose between high-quality screenshots or lightweight wireframes for most frameworks.
You pay by session volume, not by feature or events tracked.
Below, we’ll dig into each of these differentiators in more detail and share how they impact your ability to find patterns and understand the why behind drop-offs, friction points, and user behavior.
Then, we’ll briefly walk through how to use session replays with UXCam, including watching and filtering through playbacks, communicating findings with your dev team, and using AI analytics to help you save time and find important patterns you didn’t know to look for.
Note: At UXCam, we also support web applications so you can gather and manage all user behavior analytics from one platform.
Built mobile-first to support Flutter, iOS, Android, and More
Many session replay platforms started as web tools and either still don’t offer mobile or mobile was added on later.
This is an issue for a few reasons:
Poor performance: Tools that were built for the web often have laggier video playback and weaker gesture capture (i.e., they miss swipes, drop multi-touch actions) when applied to mobile. You end up watching a replay that doesn’t quite match what the user actually did, so eventually you’ll end up missing important actions that are causing friction.
Platform coverage: Many session replay tools only support iOS and Android, but not cross-platform frameworks like Flutter or React Native. They also tend to be slow in adapting to new versions of the frameworks they do support.
SDK weight: A lot of mobile SDKs are 2-3 MB, which is quite heavy when you have to keep things lightweight for good mobile performance and are trying to juggle 10 to 20 SDKs without affecting the user experience (e.g., slow load times for the user, app crashes).
UXCam has focused on mobile from the beginning, and thus we’ve spent more than a decade refining our mobile SDKs . The result is that our SDK is ultralight at less than 1 MB while still offering industry-leading quality and performance . Users frequently report high-quality screen capture, fast replay, and low crash rates.
Plus, we support most mobile frameworks including Flutter, React Native, Cordova, Xamarin, NativeScript, Kotlin Multiplatform, iOS (including SwiftUI), and Android.
"UXCam was easy to integrate into our react native mobile app and the data has hugely helped us validate our proposition with users." – Kieran Fitzsimons, CEO of MySunshine
Built session-replay-first, so anyone can answer questions without waiting on devs or new sessions
In order for session recordings to be useful, you need to be able to filter and tie them to specific user actions or events.
Here are a couple of examples:
Looking at a conversion funnel, you see a drop-off on a specific page, wonder why, and look to session recordings for the answer.
Event analytics > session recordings
You notice in one user’s session that when they clicked on the pay button, they were shown an error page, and you want to know if that’s an isolated event or if it’s happening for all users on all devices. So, you filter the session recordings by error pages.
Session recording > event-based filtering
But how those event analytics were built into the platform is important. Most platforms started with event analytics and added session recordings later, which is an issue for a few reasons:
A developer has to code the event before you can track it, which is often quite time-consuming.
You can’t filter or track past session recordings by the event you just set up. So, not only do you have to wait on the developer to set up the event for you, but you’re also losing data in the meantime.
The session replay feature is an additional SDK that was bolted on later, and multiple SDKs often lead to issues like more bugs and data getting lost between session recordings and other features.
What this might look like in the examples above is not seeing the failed button click right before the user dropped off or miscounting the number of users that got the error screen.
At UXCam, we took the opposite approach and built everything on top of the session replays, which means:
You capture everything automatically from day one. You can also choose to record only some sessions for privacy or data storage reasons.
A non-technical person can create a trackable event just by clicking on something they see in an already-recorded session, no code required.
Any event you create applies to past recordings, not just new ones. So the moment you decide you care about something (e.g., a bug in the payment screen), you can immediately search existing sessions for it instead of waiting for your dev team to set it up and for new sessions with that event to roll in.
One SDK, so you can easily jump to relevant heatmaps, funnels, or any other report and know that the data will be consistent and complete.
Plus, you can ask any question in plain language and Tara AI will look into it for you.
Not only will she build the necessary reports, but she’ll also analyze session recordings and return a full report backed by evidence (specific session recordings, heatmaps, etc.), a confidence score, and recommended next steps.
Within the report, you’ll see links that take you straight to the session recordings and reports that back up her findings.
This would take a human analyst hours, but Tara can do it in minutes.
Tara also provides proactive insights. On your homepage, you’ll see reports that Tara put together without anyone lifting a finger. This helps you discover issues sooner and with less effort. Again, everything is backed up with real user sessions and data.
Privacy controls that support GDPR and company data-privacy requirements
When it comes to GDPR requirements and your company policies regarding data privacy, there are a few things to look for.
Options for masking personally identifiable information (PII)
With many tools, you’ll either have to use a wireframe representation of each screen instead of full screenshots (more on this in the next section) or manually mark each area of the UI that needs to be masked, which is not only tedious but leaves more room for error.
At UXCam, we automatically mask or blur sensitive data for you, and you have a few options for how it’s done.
You can mask all text fields, certain sections of the screen, or the entire screen.
Or, with our unique Blur API, you can adjust the strength and radius of the blur.
And you can set different rules for each screen for maximum visibility without compromising on security.
Data storage options
Many platforms offer only one data-hosting region. UXCam lets you choose servers in the EU, USA, or UAE, helping you meet applicable data-residency requirements and internal policies.
Signed data processing agreement (DPA)
A DPA is the contract that outlines how a vendor is allowed and required to handle sensitive data. It’s a requirement for GDPR compliance, but not all companies are willing to sign one.
We sign a DPA with every business we work with.
You can delete user data, discard IP addresses, provide customers with a copy of their data, and/or include an opt-in/-out functionality based on your company’s and country’s requirements.
We hold SOC 2 Type II certification.
All user data is encrypted at rest and in transit.
We never sell your information to any third party, including advertisers.
Choose between high-quality screenshots and efficient wireframes
There are two main ways to capture a session recording: screenshots or wireframes.
Screenshots produce a video-like recording that shows everything the user saw, including graphics/images, text, and colors. This makes it easier to identify friction points and improve the user experience, but it produces larger files.
Wireframes use generic icons and shapes to indicate the various pieces of the UI. This is lighter weight and, as discussed above, is the only option some platforms offer for masking sensitive data. But it sometimes misses animations or custom UI elements.
Some tools only offer one or the other, but we let you choose either one for all supported frameworks.
Pricing based on sessions, not features, so you always have the tools and support you need
Many product analytics platforms charge extra if you need help with onboarding, tutorials on more advanced setups, and ongoing technical or live support calls. This can add up fast, especially if the tool is complicated to set up (like many event-based tools are).
And some platforms charge separately for different features or group different features by tiers, which may leave you paying extra for things you don’t need just to get the basics that you do need.
At UXCam, we keep pricing simple and base it on your monthly session volume. Beyond that, everything is included, from basic session replay features to AI analysis to ongoing, live support.
Plus, you can test everything out for free for the first 3k session recordings, no credit card required.
Viewing Session Recordings with UXCam
Every mobile session in UXCam is recorded automatically, so you can watch every tap, swipe, and screen transition that a user did or saw played back like a video.
Note: You can also choose to sample sessions.
When you open Sessions, you’ll land on a page with two tabs. The first is a list of each recording.
The second is the analytics tab that allows you to zoom out and identify patterns in user recordings and keep tabs on things like overall session health, volume over time, recurring issues, and more.
With both tabs, you can apply nearly any filter you want. The most common filters like session duration, rage taps, or location are built-in, but you can also create custom filters based on unique identifiers or specific actions.
You can also simply describe the type of filter you want or the question you have, and our AI assistant, Tara , will create the necessary filter for you.
At the top of the session replay screen, you’ll see a customizable header that you can configure to display anything, from the user’s device to their location to custom events that you create.
Along the bottom of the screen is the playback toolbar and a color-coded session timeline.
Rage taps, UI freezes, and any custom event you create are all marked so you can jump straight to the moments that you care about.
The settings button allows you to change the playback speed and toggle on the skip inactivity feature, which automatically skips moments when the user is reading, distracted, or not directly interacting with your app.
You’ll also see forward and backward buttons, which allow you to skip to other sessions performed by that same user without going back to the list.
To the right of the replay, there are two tabs:
User journey, which includes every session for that user written out with timestamps
Properties, which includes all user details including device, network and location, time, and custom user properties.
Finally, you can easily leave comments for your team that stay attached to the session recording, download the recording, share a link with anyone (with options for controlled access such as whether they’ll be required to sign in or not), and create a Jira ticket — all from right within the session replay screen.
Ready to see UXCam in action on your own app? Schedule a demo or sign up for a free trial and start recording sessions within 5 minutes.
Contentsquare (Hotjar and Heap)
Contentsquare acquired Heap and Hotjar, and both are now part of its broader platform. Hotjar’s plans now route through Contentsquare, while Heap still maintains its own site and pricing.
The platform brings together Hotjar's qualitative tools (heatmaps, session recordings, surveys), Heap's product analytics with retroactive event capture, and Contentsquare's enterprise behavioral analytics and new AI features. While it supports mobile, the main focus is web apps.
The free tier is unusually generous, with autocapture for up to 200,000 analyzed sessions per month and up to 10,000 session replay captures.
However, many teams find that it has a steep learning curve.
Amplitude is an event analytics platform at its core, with features such as event tracking, event segmentation, funnels, retention, cohorts, and user-journey analysis.
Amplitude added Session Replay after its core analytics tools, launching it for web applications before expanding to mobile.
It's now generally available and integrated with Amplitude Analytics, so you can move between quantitative data and the replays behind it.
Once set up, Amplitude is a powerful platform. But like any event-based tool, software engineers can spend months setting it up only to realize they haven’t quite done it right and aren’t capturing the behaviors that matter.
Amplitude bases its pricing on events rather than sessions, so the bill tends to follow instrumentation maturity rather than customer count.
Fullstory is a behavioral data platform best known for high-fidelity session replay, paired with product analytics, funnels, heatmaps, and frustration signals.
Its "Fullcapture" technology logs every click, scroll, and page mutation without manual event tagging, so you can retroactively analyze data and answer questions you didn't know you had when the data was collected.
Founded in Atlanta in 2014 by a team out of Google, Fullstory grew up analyzing websites. It supports mobile, but mobile capture sits on paid plans, and the platform's focus is web. Its StoryAI layer uses Google's Gemini and Vertex AI to surface rage clicks, form errors, and friction across sessions automatically.
Fullstory uses a session-based pricing model.
Microsoft Clarity
Microsoft Clarity is a free session replay and heatmap tool. It started on web and later expanded into mobile, with SDKs now covering Android, iOS, Flutter, and React Native. Rather than capturing actual video, its mobile SDK reconstructs walkthrough-style session replays from low-level drawing commands.
For zero cost, the feature list is surprisingly deep: tap heatmaps, rage/dead tap flags for spotting friction, device and OS-level segmentation, and AI-written session summaries. Setup is simple enough that most teams are up and running the same day.
The catch shows up in a few places:
Dev tools: Clarity doesn’t provide replay-level console logs. It includes built-in crash/error analytics on Android and can link replays to Firebase Crashlytics for more detailed crash reports.
Compliance and support: There's no paid support tier to fall back on. Teams with HIPAA or enterprise governance requirements should confirm whether Clarity’s controls and terms meet their needs.
Shared data: Microsoft says it doesn't sell the data Clarity collects, but Microsoft and Clarity can access it. Teams should review the applicable terms and privacy statement before implementation.
LogRocket is a session replay tool built for developers that also includes some UX analytics features like heatmaps, clickmaps, and scrollmaps. It includes DOM playback, console and network logs, and performance monitoring (e.g., Core Web Vitals, CPU usage), all synced to the exact moments when they occurred in the recording.
It covers mobile through native iOS and Android SDKs, plus React Native and Flutter.
However, feature support varies by platform, with some web features unavailable on mobile.
Galileo, its AI layer, watches sessions and automatically surfaces friction and technical issues.
Teams can turn flagged issues into Jira tickets, track pull requests through GitHub, or dispatch Cursor or Claude agents.
LogRocket prices based on monthly session volume rather than events. Its current pricing page advertises a 14-day free trial, while unlimited seats are listed as an Enterprise feature.
Datadog is a digital experience monitoring tool built for engineers with an extensive suite of tools that cover infrastructure management, app performance, data monitoring, and log management.
They support iOS and Android and offer features specifically for mobile application monitoring including performance optimization reports, crash alerts and investigation tools, and user journey recording of every tap, swipe, and scroll.
Mobile Session Replay is part of Datadog RUM rather than a standalone replay-only product.
PostHog is a developer-first platform that bundles session replay alongside product analytics, feature flags, error tracking, and experiments.
Mobile replay covers native iOS and Android, React Native, and Flutter, though PostHog is upfront that web has the most complete feature support.
Native iOS and Android use wireframe mode by default and can switch to screenshot mode, while React Native and Flutter always use screenshot mode.
Mobile replay also doesn’t capture keyboard input.
Mobile recordings include console logs and network monitoring, so engineers can trace an issue without leaving the recording. However, the DOM explorer is only available for web recordings. AI-generated session summaries surface key moments automatically, so you're not stuck watching every session start to finish.
Pricing is usage-based, with web and mobile recordings billed separately. The free tier includes 5,000 web recordings and 2,500 mobile recordings per month. The cost per recording decreases as volume increases, and pricing is not seat-based.
Sentry is focused mostly on error monitoring and observability, so session replay just supports those features. Coverage spans web and mobile (Android, iOS, React Native, Flutter), with replay running on both UIKit and SwiftUI.
Like most of these tools, session recordings are tied to crash reports, network requests, and console entries, so engineers can see both what the user saw and what the app was doing behind the scenes.
By default, mobile replay masks all text, images, and user input at the device level before anything leaves it, and Sentry offers a DPA covering GDPR/CCPA for replay data.
Pricing is usage-based and billed per replay alongside Sentry's other event types (errors, spans, logs), with a free developer tier and new users getting 5,000 free replays a month for their first three months before standard quota pricing kicks in.
Embrace is a mobile-first observability platform that also supports web apps and combines crash reporting, ANR detection, network monitoring, real user monitoring, and user timelines.
User timelines provide a detailed overview of a user’s session, but they aren’t video-like playbacks.
Embrace says they serve a similar purpose and capture 100% of user sessions without sampling.
They support most mobile frameworks including Unity, and they tend to serve larger, mobile-first engineering teams rather than startups.
You can reach out to Embrace for pricing.
Finally, Embrace entered into a definitive agreement to be acquired by Palo Alto Networks in July 2026, so some features and functionality may change.
Still not sure which tool fits your stack? If you're a product team trying to understand why users are taking certain actions, start with UXCam. Schedule a demo and/or get set up in 5 minutes , no dev help required, and see the sessions behind your own funnel for free.

The second is the analytics tab that allows you to zoom out and identify patterns in user recordings and keep tabs on things like overall session health, volume over time, recurring issues, and more.

With both tabs, you can apply nearly any filter you want. The most common filters like session duration, rage taps, or location are built-in, but you can also create custom filters based on unique identifiers or specific actions.
You can also simply describe the type of filter you want or the question you have, and our AI assistant, Tara , will create the necessary filter for you.
At the top of the session replay screen, you’ll see a customizable header that you can configure to display anything, from the user’s device to their location to custom events that you create.
Along the bottom of the screen is the playback toolbar and a color-coded session timeline.
Rage taps, UI freezes, and any custom event you create are all marked so you can jump straight to the moments that you care about.

The settings button allows you to change the playback speed and toggle on the skip inactivity feature, which automatically skips moments when the user is reading, distracted, or not directly interacting with your app.
You’ll also see forward and backward buttons, which allow you to skip to other sessions performed by that same user without going back to the list.
To the right of the replay, there are two tabs:
User journey, which includes every session for that user written out with timestamps
Properties, which includes all user details including device, network and location, time, and custom user properties.

Finally, you can easily leave comments for your team that stay attached to the session recording, download the recording, share a link with anyone (with options for controlled access such as whether they’ll be required to sign in or not), and create a Jira ticket — all from right within the session replay screen.
Ready to see UXCam in action on your own app? Schedule a demo or sign up for a free trial and start recording sessions within 5 minutes.
Contentsquare (Hotjar and Heap)
Contentsquare acquired Heap and Hotjar, and both are now part of its broader platform. Hotjar’s plans now route through Contentsquare, while Heap still maintains its own site and pricing.

The platform brings together Hotjar's qualitative tools (heatmaps, session recordings, surveys), Heap's product analytics with retroactive event capture, and Contentsquare's enterprise behavioral analytics and new AI features. While it supports mobile, the main focus is web apps.
The free tier is unusually generous, with autocapture for up to 200,000 analyzed sessions per month and up to 10,000 session replay captures.
However, many teams find that it has a steep learning curve.
Amplitude is an event analytics platform at its core, with features such as event tracking, event segmentation, funnels, retention, cohorts, and user-journey analysis.
Amplitude added Session Replay after its core analytics tools, launching it for web applications before expanding to mobile.
It's now generally available and integrated with Amplitude Analytics, so you can move between quantitative data and the replays behind it.

Once set up, Amplitude is a powerful platform. But like any event-based tool, software engineers can spend months setting it up only to realize they haven’t quite done it right and aren’t capturing the behaviors that matter.
Amplitude bases its pricing on events rather than sessions, so the bill tends to follow instrumentation maturity rather than customer count.
Fullstory is a behavioral data platform best known for high-fidelity session replay, paired with product analytics, funnels, heatmaps, and frustration signals.

Its "Fullcapture" technology logs every click, scroll, and page mutation without manual event tagging, so you can retroactively analyze data and answer questions you didn't know you had when the data was collected.

Founded in Atlanta in 2014 by a team out of Google, Fullstory grew up analyzing websites. It supports mobile, but mobile capture sits on paid plans, and the platform's focus is web. Its StoryAI layer uses Google's Gemini and Vertex AI to surface rage clicks, form errors, and friction across sessions automatically.
Fullstory uses a session-based pricing model.
Microsoft Clarity

Microsoft Clarity is a free session replay and heatmap tool. It started on web and later expanded into mobile, with SDKs now covering Android, iOS, Flutter, and React Native. Rather than capturing actual video, its mobile SDK reconstructs walkthrough-style session replays from low-level drawing commands.

For zero cost, the feature list is surprisingly deep: tap heatmaps, rage/dead tap flags for spotting friction, device and OS-level segmentation, and AI-written session summaries. Setup is simple enough that most teams are up and running the same day.
The catch shows up in a few places:
Dev tools: Clarity doesn’t provide replay-level console logs. It includes built-in crash/error analytics on Android and can link replays to Firebase Crashlytics for more detailed crash reports.
Compliance and support: There's no paid support tier to fall back on. Teams with HIPAA or enterprise governance requirements should confirm whether Clarity’s controls and terms meet their needs.
Shared data: Microsoft says it doesn't sell the data Clarity collects, but Microsoft and Clarity can access it. Teams should review the applicable terms and privacy statement before implementation.

LogRocket is a session replay tool built for developers that also includes some UX analytics features like heatmaps, clickmaps, and scrollmaps. It includes DOM playback, console and network logs, and performance monitoring (e.g., Core Web Vitals, CPU usage), all synced to the exact moments when they occurred in the recording.
It covers mobile through native iOS and Android SDKs, plus React Native and Flutter.
However, feature support varies by platform, with some web features unavailable on mobile.
Galileo, its AI layer, watches sessions and automatically surfaces friction and technical issues.
Teams can turn flagged issues into Jira tickets, track pull requests through GitHub, or dispatch Cursor or Claude agents.
LogRocket prices based on monthly session volume rather than events. Its current pricing page advertises a 14-day free trial, while unlimited seats are listed as an Enterprise feature.
Datadog is a digital experience monitoring tool built for engineers with an extensive suite of tools that cover infrastructure management, app performance, data monitoring, and log management.

They support iOS and Android and offer features specifically for mobile application monitoring including performance optimization reports, crash alerts and investigation tools, and user journey recording of every tap, swipe, and scroll.
Mobile Session Replay is part of Datadog RUM rather than a standalone replay-only product.
PostHog is a developer-first platform that bundles session replay alongside product analytics, feature flags, error tracking, and experiments.
Mobile replay covers native iOS and Android, React Native, and Flutter, though PostHog is upfront that web has the most complete feature support.
Native iOS and Android use wireframe mode by default and can switch to screenshot mode, while React Native and Flutter always use screenshot mode.
Mobile replay also doesn’t capture keyboard input.

Mobile recordings include console logs and network monitoring, so engineers can trace an issue without leaving the recording. However, the DOM explorer is only available for web recordings. AI-generated session summaries surface key moments automatically, so you're not stuck watching every session start to finish.

Pricing is usage-based, with web and mobile recordings billed separately. The free tier includes 5,000 web recordings and 2,500 mobile recordings per month. The cost per recording decreases as volume increases, and pricing is not seat-based.

Sentry is focused mostly on error monitoring and observability, so session replay just supports those features. Coverage spans web and mobile (Android, iOS, React Native, Flutter), with replay running on both UIKit and SwiftUI.

Like most of these tools, session recordings are tied to crash reports, network requests, and console entries, so engineers can see both what the user saw and what the app was doing behind the scenes.
By default, mobile replay masks all text, images, and user input at the device level before anything leaves it, and Sentry offers a DPA covering GDPR/CCPA for replay data.

Pricing is usage-based and billed per replay alongside Sentry's other event types (errors, spans, logs), with a free developer tier and new users getting 5,000 free replays a month for their first three months before standard quota pricing kicks in.
Embrace is a mobile-first observability platform that also supports web apps and combines crash reporting, ANR detection, network monitoring, real user monitoring, and user timelines.
User timelines provide a detailed overview of a user’s session, but they aren’t video-like playbacks.
Embrace says they serve a similar purpose and capture 100% of user sessions without sampling.
They support most mobile frameworks including Unity, and they tend to serve larger, mobile-first engineering teams rather than startups.
You can reach out to Embrace for pricing.
Finally, Embrace entered into a definitive agreement to be acquired by Palo Alto Networks in July 2026, so some features and functionality may change.
